result.markdown: --- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.topological_generations()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: Group the nodes of a DAG into topological generations. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.topological_generations()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | Edgecase description: Group the nodes of a DAG into topological generations. title: >- [Graph.topological_generations()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Group the nodes of a DAG into topological generations. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Group the nodes of a DAG into topological generations. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L57334-L57394){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.topological_generations() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Topological generations](../assets/graphs/topological-generations.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A seven-node DAG laid out in four columns, one per generation, each in its own color and tinted region: the sources A, B (accent), then C, D (teal), E, F (violet), and finally G (gold). Every arrow points to a later generation. The card lists the generations 0 to 3." width="100%"} Generation 0 holds the nodes with no incoming edges (the sources). Removing them leaves a new set of sources, which form generation 1, and so on. A node's generation is therefore the number of edges on the *longest* path that reaches it from a source. Nodes in the same generation never depend on one another, which makes generations the natural schedule for parallel work: every task in a generation can run at once, as soon as the previous generation has finished. They are also the layers of a layered (Sugiyama-style) drawing of the DAG. Every ordering that lists the generations in sequence is a valid topological order, as returned by `topological_sort()`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : One list of node IDs per generation, in order, each sorted by ID. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is undirected or contains a cycle. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} In this build pipeline, `fetch` comes first; `compile` and `docs` can then run in parallel; `test` waits for `compile`, and `package` waits for `test`: ::: {#c78d76b7 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["fetch", "compile", "test", "package", "docs"]) .add_edges([ ("fetch", "compile"), ("compile", "test"), ("test", "package"), ("compile", "package"), ("fetch", "docs"), ]) ) [[graph.get_label_from_id(n) for n in gen] for gen in graph.topological_generations()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [['fetch'], ['compile', 'docs'], ['test'], ['package']] ``` ::: :::
